summary_html: Agency decides to **remove a child immediately** due to **imminent danger** prior to a court order. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) requires later **court findings** on reasonable efforts; constitutional limits (due process; search/seizure) apply.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E (42 U.S.C. §§ 670–679c)** — reasonable-efforts findings; permanency timelines  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — monitors safety & removal decision quality

provisions_triggered.name: Due Process / Law of the Land

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: In an Oregon case, the court held city police officers who assisted an ORS 419B.150 removal at the direction of Oregon DHS were entitled to qualified immunity because their reliance on the agency's protective-custody determination was objectively reasonable.
key_cases.relevance: Shows that the constitutionality of the removal decision itself remains with the agency officials who made it, while assisting officers are judged on the reasonableness of their reliance.
key_cases.quote: Sjurset correctly points out, however, that an officer cannot blindly rely on the existence of a protective-custody determination to avoid liability.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: Sitting en banc, the court held a genuine dispute existed as to whether a newborn was in imminent danger justifying warrantless removal, because social workers may not forgo a warrant if they had adequate time to obtain one without risking the child.
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling en banc statement in Oregon's circuit that available time to seek a warrant defeats any claim of exigency in a removal.
key_cases.quote: under Rogers, the social workers here lacked cause to forgo a warrant if they had adequate time to pursue one through the ordinary judicial process

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held that a social worker and police officer were not entitled to qualified immunity for a coerced warrantless entry into a home to investigate suspected child abuse, or for the strip search of a three-year-old, because the Fourth Amendment applies to child-abuse investigations.
key_cases.relevance: Rejects the argument that any child-welfare check is automatically an exigent circumstance.
key_cases.quote: It does not hold that the social worker may enter the home despite the absence of consent or exigency.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held a social worker was not entitled to summary judgment on a warrantless-seizure claim because officials must obtain prior judicial authorization before removing a child absent reasonable cause to believe the child faces imminent danger of serious bodily injury.
key_cases.relevance: This is the Ninth Circuit's canonical formulation of the imminent-danger exception to the warrant requirement for child removal, including the scope limitation.
key_cases.quote: Government officials are required to obtain prior judicial authorization before intruding on a parent's custody of her child unless they possess information at the time of the seizure

key_cases.case_name: Scanlon v. County of Los Angeles
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held the agency's statement of cause supporting a protective custody warrant contained material misrepresentations and omissions such that a reasonable magistrate informed of the true facts would not have issued it, and remanded the judicial-deception claim.
key_cases.relevance: Establishes that obtaining a removal warrant does not immunize the agency if the supporting application misstates or omits material facts.
key_cases.quote: We conclude that the Statement contained misrepresentations and omissions of fact and so remand to the district court.

key_cases.case_name: Dept. of Human Services v. M. P.
key_cases.holding: The court held a protective custody order under ORS 419B.150 is not an 'initial child custody determination' and the supporting declaration is not the first pleading, so the dependency proceeding commenced when the petition was filed, defeating UCCJEA home-state jurisdiction.
key_cases.relevance: Explains precisely what an ex parte 'pick-up order' does and does not accomplish, including that no notice to parents is required before or after issuance.
key_cases.quote: An issued but unexecuted protective custody order does not trigger the juvenile court's jurisdiction or commence any time period during which a petition must be filed.
